Scotland does not use the Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS). Criminal record checks, called disclosures, are handled by Disclosure Scotland. The levels are Level 1, Level 2, Level 2 with barred list check, and membership of the Protecting Vulnerable Groups (PVG) scheme.

Disclosure Scotland has a process for transgender and non-binary applicants. You only need it if your employer is countersigning your application. A Level 1 disclosure does not show previous names, so if you apply for one without a countersignatory, you can include them when asked.

With the process, you use your present name and gender on the application and leave out previous names linked to your transition. If you are non-binary, you still need to choose male or female on the form. Disclosure Scotland says this does not need to be your legal sex, and it is not used to match you to criminal records.

The Department for Communities handles benefits in Northern Ireland.

evisa:
UK eVisa and UKVI Update your UKVI account when your name or gender marker changes. Some changes can be made online. Others need UKVI to make them for you, or mean replacing a physical visa, which has a fee.

You can update your name in your UKVI account online, using an identity document that shows your new name, such as your updated passport. GOV.UK says you cannot change your name while you are waiting for a decision on a visa application.

How you change your gender marker depends on your situation, and GOV.UK has separate guidance for each. For example, if you still have a physical visa and your stay in the UK is longer than 6 months, you must replace it with an eVisa when your name or gender changes, and there is a fee. If you are outside the UK, you may need to ask UKVI to update your account for you and give your fingerprints and photo at a visa application centre.

If your home country will not change your passport, the Home Office says it can still show your new name and gender on your eVisa, as long as you can show you use them for all purposes. Under the EU Settlement Scheme, for example, it asks for a letter from your country's embassy or consulate confirming it will not make the change, plus a GRC or medical evidence. Rainbow Migration can help with situations like this.

⚠️ Travel note: Make sure the name on your travel ticket matches your passport. Border Force and airlines may also check documents such as your eVisa. Mismatches can lead to delays or difficulties when travelling.

grc_docs:
Paperwork for your GRC application As well as the medical reports and the two years of evidence, the application asks for a statutory declaration, your full birth or adoption certificate, and copies of anything showing a change of name.

These are the documents the application asks for besides the medical reports and the evidence of living in your affirmed gender. You can usually send copies, but keep the originals, as the panel may ask to see them after you apply.

Statutory declaration: GOV.UK provides the declaration itself, along with guidance on which version applies to you and who can witness your signature.

Birth or adoption certificate: an original or certified copy of the full certificate. If your birth or adoption was registered in the UK and you do not have it to hand, you can order a copy.

Name-change documents: if you have changed your name, you need copies of everything showing when you did so. This includes both enrolled and unenrolled deed polls, and statutory declarations of a name change. These copies do not need to be certified. The name on a GRC cannot be changed after it is issued, so if you want your new name on it, change your name before you apply.

If you have ever been married or in a civil partnership: you also need copies of every marriage or civil partnership certificate. If you are currently in one and intend to stay in it, your spouse or civil partner completes a statutory declaration of their own. If a marriage or civil partnership has ended, you need the decree absolute, final order, or your partner's death certificate instead.

If any document is not in English: it needs a translation. The translator does not need any qualifications, so a friend or family member can do it, and you send both the original and the translation.

grc_med.regions.default:
Medical proof for GRC A GRC is the UK's legal route to having your gender legally recognised. It only ever recognises you as male or female; GOV.UK states plainly that non-binary genders are not legally recognised in the UK. The application also requires two medical reports; the GOV.UK links below have details on what is needed.

The GRC application requires two medical reports. Both must be written by either two different medical doctors registered in the UK, or a medical doctor and a clinical psychologist, both registered in the UK. A nurse practitioner cannot write either report.

The first report must come from a registered doctor or clinical psychologist who practises in the field of gender dysphoria. GOV.UK publishes a list of specialists, but says this list is not complete and not always up to date; someone not on the list can still write this report if they include a brief summary of their experience in the field.

The second report can come from any registered doctor or clinical psychologist, including a GP, a surgeon, or an endocrinologist. There is no set content for this second report. Reports do not need to be written specially for your application if you already have ones that meet these requirements.

Both reports must include the writer's name, practice address and contact details. At least one must describe any gender affirmation treatment you have had or plan to have, such as hormones or surgery, or explain why you have not had any and do not plan to.

If your gender is already legally recognised in a country or territory on GOV.UK's approved list, you can apply through the shorter overseas route instead, which does not need these medical reports. The GOV.UK links below have the application requirements, the list of specialists, and the list of recognised countries.

Update your records with HMRC. Your tax records, payslips, and benefits payments will then use the correct name and details.

i You can also ask HMRC to protect your records so fewer people can see them.

Name changes: HMRC can update your name when notified. You can also ask them to restrict access to your records for privacy. The note below explains how this works without a Gender Recognition Certificate. The HMRC team that handles this is called "Special Section D", and restricted records are looked after by "Public Department 1" (PD1). Knowing these names can help if you need to chase things up by phone. The GOV.UK link below has the details.

⚠️ If you are 16 or 17: Your National Insurance number is usually sent automatically shortly before your 16th birthday, based on your Child Benefit record, so the letter may arrive in your old name. The number itself never changes and does not need updating, but you can still tell HMRC your new name the same way as above. The GOV.UK link below has the details.

Gender marker changes: If you have a Gender Recognition Certificate (GRC), HMRC is usually notified automatically and your records are moved to a restricted file; only specialist staff can access them. HMRC has confirmed it does not change the gender marker on a record without a GRC. However, restricting your records for privacy is a separate matter from the gender marker itself.

i Some people without a GRC report that Special Section D can still apply the same restriction if asked directly, though HMRC holds no published guidance either way, so treat this as worth asking about rather than guaranteed. The GOV.UK link below has the details.

irish_passport:
Irish passport (Good Friday Agreement route) As someone born in Northern Ireland, you may be able to claim Irish citizenship under the Good Friday Agreement. The Republic of Ireland has a separate process for updating a gender marker on a passport, which differs from the UK GRC route.

Under the Good Friday Agreement, people born in Northern Ireland can choose to be Irish citizens. If you were born on or after 1 January 2005, this depends on your parents: one of them must be a British or Irish citizen, or have lived on the island of Ireland for three of the four years before your birth. The Republic of Ireland has its own gender recognition process, which works very differently from the UK GRC route. The Department of Foreign Affairs and TENI (Transgender Equality Network Ireland) links below have details on eligibility, requirements, and how to apply.

Evidence needed: If you live in Northern Ireland or anywhere else outside Ireland, the Passport Service asks for a statutory declaration stating that you have a settled and solemn intention of living in your new gender for the rest of your life, together with two documents from two different sources showing use of your new name over at least two years. The Passport Service does not accept a deed poll to change the name on an Irish passport. This applies whether you are applying for your first Irish passport or renewing one. A first application also asks for an identity verification form, your full original birth certificate showing your parents' names, proof of address dated within the last 12 months, and original government-issued photo identification.

⚠️ If you were recently issued a passport in your previous name: The Passport Service says that if you applied for and were issued a passport in your previous name during the two years before you apply, your two years of proof start again from the date that passport was issued. It may make an exception if that passport was due to expire before you could build up two years, so contact them before applying.

Note on the Irish GRC: An Irish Gender Recognition Certificate is a separate route. It is only available to people ordinarily resident in the Republic of Ireland, or whose birth, adoption, or foreign birth registration is recorded there, so it does not apply to someone living in Northern Ireland or Great Britain. It is not covered further here. The TENI link below explains the Irish GRC process for people it does apply to.

⚠️ If you are 16 or 17: the published adult guidance does not say whether this route is open to 16 and 17 year olds. If this applies to you, contact the Passport Service before applying to check what you need to do.

Your GP practice can request a new NHS number with the correct gender marker (for adults), or update your existing record. Your medical care, screening invitations, and correspondence will then use your correct details.

For gender marker updates there are two options. A new NHS number protects your privacy and stops your old name appearing on future letters. Alternatively, your gender marker can be updated on your existing NHS number.

⚠️ Waiting list note: Primary Care Support England (PCSE), which manages this on behalf of NHS England, warns in its own guidance that requesting a new NHS number can mean losing your place on any NHS waiting lists you are on. If you are mid-treatment or mid-referral, weigh this against the privacy benefit of a new number.

⚠️ A new NHS number cannot be undone: PCSE says your practice must tell you this before going ahead, and that if you later changed back you would be given a third NHS number. Your practice should also explain the other effects, such as on your old medical record and on screening.

⚠️ Screening note: Changing your gender marker may stop automatic NHS screening invitations, for example for cervical or breast screening. Ask your GP to check you are enrolled in the screening programmes right for your body.

Non-binary gender markers: In England, you can ask your GP to record your gender as 'indeterminate' (shown as 'Not specified' in most NHS systems) if you are 18 or over. Ask the practice to use gender code 'I' if they are unsure what to enter.

Student finance: In Scotland this is handled by SAAS (Student Awards Agency for Scotland). Unlike the rest of the UK, SAAS uses a single combined form to update your name, gender, and title together, accepting a deed poll, statutory declaration, GRC, or several other kinds of evidence. Universities: Most offer free replacement certificates, though some charge a small admin fee.

Exam boards and awarding bodies (e.g. Pearson, which awards BTECs, or City & Guilds): Each awarding body has its own process and fees. Some charge a significant fee per replacement certificate. ${CN} A few people have had this fee waived just by contacting the board directly and explaining the situation, though it is not publicly documented, so it is worth asking rather than assuming you have to pay.

Professional and vocational bodies: Regulated professions such as nursing (NMC) and medicine (GMC) have a single UK-wide regulator, each with their own update process. Others are regulated separately by nation: solicitors, for example, are regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority in England and Wales, the Law Society of Scotland, or the Law Society of Northern Ireland, depending on where you are registered. Most have handled these requests before.

ukpass:
UK passport

For a name change, your deed poll and evidence of using your new name (such as a bank statement or utility bill) will be needed. For a gender marker change without a GRC, HMPO also asks for a letter from you asking for the change of gender, a letter from a medical professional (such as your GP or a gender specialist) confirming the change is likely to be permanent, and evidence that you use your name and gender for all purposes, such as a bank statement, utility bill or payslip. This applies even if your name is not changing. HMPO may also ask for someone who knows you to confirm your identity, unless it can match your photo to your previous passport. If you already have a GRC, HMPO does not usually ask for these letters or for evidence of use.

⚠️ Medical letter: HMPO is strict about what this letter must include. According to HMPO's published guidance, it should:

  • Be written by either a medical professional registered with the General Medical Council (GMC) or the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC), or a medical professional, in the UK or overseas, who is not registered with either body but who can provide evidence of their qualifications and experience. HMPO gives examples including GPs, gender dysphoria clinicians and specialists, clinical psychologists, consultant psychologists and psychiatrists, practitioner psychologists, and specialist nurses, though this is not a complete list
  • Be dated and include the medical professional's handwritten signature
  • Confirm that the medical professional knows you well enough to make a diagnosis
  • State your name and specified gender
  • Confirm you use your name and gender for all purposes
  • State that your gender change is "likely to be permanent"

If HMPO rejects a letter from a medical professional who is not registered with the GMC or HCPC, it will ask for a new letter from one who is registered. Treat the wider route as a fallback, not the easiest option.

The GOV.UK link below has the full requirements.

⚠️ If you are 16 or 17: unlike a name-only change, a gender marker change usually needs the consent of everyone with parental responsibility for you. If you cannot get it, send HMPO a letter explaining why, and it will consider an exception. The exceptions include being within two weeks of turning 18 (HMPO holds your application until your birthday), your parents having died, having no contact with one or both parents, and being in contact with your parents but unable to get their consent. Each case is decided individually: HMPO may ask for evidence such as details of your care arrangements or a statutory declaration, and if it issues the passport without consent, your parents can object. If asking for consent would put you at risk, tell HMPO: it will ask for any evidence from the police or another organisation such as social services, and get advice from its safeguarding team. Contact HMPO directly to find out what applies to you.

⚠️ Travel note: Make sure the name on your travel ticket matches your passport. Border Force and airlines may check documents including any eVisa. Mismatches can lead to delays or difficulties when travelling.

⚠️ Non-binary marker: UK passports currently only offer M or F: there is no X or non-binary option. You can still note your identity in a covering letter or in the additional information section of your application. If you do, HMPO will phone you to explain that it can only print M or F, and to ask for your current gender, male or female. If that is different from your last passport, HMPO treats it as a change of gender, which needs the evidence above. If you cannot answer straight away, you have 7 days to call back, or your application may be withdrawn.

Vehicle logbook (V5C): The V5C is the document that records the registered keeper of a vehicle. There is no fee for a name change.

This is a separate process from updating your driving licence. Even if your licence is already updated, the V5C is held on a different record and will need to be updated separately.

⚠️ Legal requirement: Telling the DVLA about a name change is not optional for a vehicle keeper as you can face a large fine for not doing so.
